title: Deploys: Canary, Blue-Green, Flags
subtitle: Watch one new version ship by rolling, blue-green, canary, flags and shadow traffic, and see how far a bad build can spread in each.
learn: How rolling, blue-green, and canary deploys differ in cost, speed, and blast radius
Why a canary only limits damage if automatic metric checks compare it with v1
How feature flags separate deploying code from releasing a feature
What a dark launch (shadow traffic) tests that staging cannot
How expand/contract migrations keep the database safe while two versions run at once

steps.title: Shipping without breaking things
steps.body: Your team has a new build, v2, and 40 servers running v1 for millions of users. Every deploy is a bet that v2 behaves in production like it did in tests, and sometimes the bet loses. So the real question is not how to deploy. It is how many users a bad change can hurt (the blast radius) and how fast you can undo it. On the diagram, all traffic still goes to v1 while v2 waits.
steps.idea: Deploy strategy is risk management: limit how many users a bad build reaches and how fast you can undo it.
steps.caption: All traffic is on v1. v2 is built and waiting.

steps.title: Rolling: swap servers in batches
steps.body: A rolling deploy swaps v1 servers for v2 a few at a time, for example 4 of 40 per batch. Between batches it waits for health checks (automatic probes that ask a server 'are you ready?'). It needs little or no spare capacity and is the default in most orchestrators. The catch: while it runs, both versions serve users, so a bad v2 keeps reaching more users batch after batch unless a check stops it. The two versions also share APIs, queues and caches, so keep those backward compatible. Rolling back means rolling forward again with the old build, which is slow.
steps.idea: Rolling is cheap and simple, but old and new run together and rollback is slow.
steps.caption: First batch done: 4 of 40 servers run v2, so 10% of traffic hits v2.

steps.title: Blue-green: flip a whole environment
steps.body: Blue-green keeps two full environments. Blue (v1) serves users while green (v2) is started and smoke-tested with no real traffic. Then the router flips 100% of traffic to green in one step, as the animation shows. Rolling back is just flipping back, often within seconds, because blue is still running. The price is paying for roughly double capacity during the switch, and the flip exposes everyone at once.
steps.idea: Blue-green gives instant rollback at the cost of double capacity and an all-at-once switch.
steps.caption: The router flips every request from v1 to v2 in one move.

steps.title: Canary: a small slice first
steps.body: A canary sends a small slice of real traffic, say 5%, to v2 while 95% stays on v1, with each user kept on one version. (The name comes from the canary once carried into coal mines as an early warning.) Automation compares v2 with v1 on the same signals: error rate, p99 latency (99% of requests finish faster than this, so it shows the slow tail), and saturation (how close servers are to their limits). Give it enough requests to be meaningful. If v2 stays within a set margin of v1 (for example errors within 0.1 points) for 10 minutes, the share steps up to 25%, 50%, then 100%.
steps.idea: A canary tests v2 on real traffic while capping the blast radius, but only if the metric comparison is automatic.
steps.caption: 5% of requests reach v2, and both versions are measured side by side.

steps.title: The canary catches a bad build
steps.body: Suppose v2 has a bug that breaks 5% of its own requests. At 5% traffic the fleet-wide error rate only creeps from 0.2% to about 0.44%, which is easy to miss on a dashboard. But v2's own error rate is 25 times v1's, so the comparison trips within two minutes and the router drops v2 back to 0%. Only about 0.25% of all requests failed (5% reached v2 and 5% of those failed), for two minutes. A blue-green flip would have sent 100% of traffic to the bad build until someone noticed, and a rolling deploy with no metric checks would have kept replacing servers.
steps.idea: Small blast radius plus automatic rollback turns an outage into a blip.
steps.caption: v2 errors spike; the router pulls all traffic back to v1.

steps.title: Feature flags: deploy is not release
steps.body: A feature flag is an on/off switch checked in code at run time, such as if flags.enabled('new-checkout', user). Here v2 is already on every server, but the new-checkout feature is switched on for only 1% of users. You can widen it to staff, then 1%, then everyone, with no new deploy, and turning it off takes seconds, not a rebuild. The cost: flags add code paths to test, and old flags pile up, so remove each one when its rollout is done. Note the Users on v2 tile counts who runs the v2 code (everyone), not who sees the feature (1%).
steps.idea: Flags decouple deploying code from releasing a feature, giving per-user control and a seconds-long kill switch.
steps.caption: All traffic runs v2, but the new-checkout flag is on for only 1% of users.

steps.title: Dark launch: run it, hide the result
steps.body: A dark launch (also called traffic mirroring) copies live requests to v2 and throws away its responses, so users only ever see v1's answers. In the animation the router sends each request to v1 for the real answer and sends a copy to v2. You learn how v2 handles real traffic and volume, such as holding a p99 of 180 ms, and you can compare its answers with v1's. (Some teams use the term for flag-hidden features instead.) The shadow path must not send emails, charge cards or write shared data. Keep the mirror asynchronous and sampled, so it cannot slow real requests or overload shared dependencies.
steps.idea: Shadow traffic tests v2 on real load without exposing users, as long as the mirror is isolated and has no side effects.
steps.caption: Mirrored copies go to v2, but only v1's responses return to users.

steps.title: The database must serve both versions
steps.body: Mid-rollout, say half the servers run v2 and half run v1, and both share one database that you cannot switch in an instant. Suppose v2 renames the name column to full_name. Use expand/contract, in separate deploys. 1) Expand: add a nullable (allowed to be empty) full_name column, which v1 ignores. 2) Deploy v2, which writes both columns but still reads name. 3) Once no v1 remains, backfill (fill the new column for existing rows) and check it is complete. 4) A later deploy switches reads to full_name. 5) Contract: drop name only when rolling back to old code is off the table.
steps.idea: Never ship a schema change that breaks the old version; add first, migrate, and remove in a separate later deploy.
steps.caption: Half the servers run each version, and both share one database.

steps.title: Pick by blast radius and rollback speed
steps.body: Rolling is cheap but slow to undo. Blue-green undoes in seconds but costs double capacity and flips everyone at once. Canary limits exposure but needs good metrics. Flags give per-user control after the deploy, and dark launches test real load without exposing users. Underneath all of them, expand/contract keeps the database working for both versions. Mature teams combine them: canary the build, flag the feature.
steps.idea: Combine canary for the build, flags for the feature, and expand/contract for the data.
steps.caption: Each tool limits risk at a different layer.

quiz.q: Your service is stateless, you have no spare capacity budget, and a few minutes of mixed versions is fine. Which strategy fits best?
options: Blue-green, because it is always safest
Dark launch to production
Rolling deploy in small batches with health checks
Canary with a full duplicate fleet
quiz.why: Rolling needs little or no extra capacity. Blue-green requires roughly double the servers during the switch, which this team has ruled out.

quiz.q: A canary at 5% traffic shows v2's error rate at 4% and v1's at 0.2%, but the fleet-wide error rate looks normal. What should happen?
options: Continue; the overall rate is fine
Roll back, because the comparison is v2 against v1, not the fleet average
Wait an hour for the numbers to average out
Raise the canary to 50% to get more data
quiz.why: At 5% share, a broken v2 is diluted in the fleet average. The canary only works when you compare the canary group directly against the baseline.

quiz.q: A bug is found in a new feature already live for 100% of users behind a flag. What is the fastest fix?
options: Roll the entire deploy back
Start a blue-green switch
Wait for the next release train
Flip the flag off
quiz.why: The flag decouples release from deploy, so turning it off takes seconds and needs no new build. Other unrelated changes in the deploy stay live.

quiz.q: You want to rename a column from name to full_name. Which plan is safe while v1 and v2 run together?
options: Add full_name, write both, backfill once v1 is gone, switch reads, and drop name in a later deploy
Rename it in the same deploy that ships v2
Drop name first, then deploy v2
Take the site down and rename it
quiz.why: A direct rename breaks whichever version expects the other column name. Expand/contract keeps both versions working and delays the destructive step until rollback is no longer needed.

quiz.q: What does a dark launch tell you that a canary does not?
options: Whether users like the new feature
Whether the database schema is correct
How v2 behaves under production-shaped load with no user ever seeing its responses
Nothing; it is the same thing
quiz.why: A dark launch mirrors traffic and discards v2's output, so users never see its responses. A canary serves real responses to a small group of users.

cheatsheet.def: Replace instances in batches with health checks between them. Little or no extra capacity; old and new coexist; rollback is another rollout.
Two full environments; flip the router to switch. Instant rollback, about 2x capacity during the switch, all users move at once.
Send a small share (1-5%) of real traffic to the new version, compare its metrics with the old, then step up. Needs automatic checks.
How many users or requests a bad change can affect before it is stopped. Deploy strategy is mainly about shrinking this.
A runtime switch that turns code paths on per user or percentage. Decouples deploy from release; remove stale flags.
Also called traffic mirroring. Copy live traffic to the new version, discard its responses, compare with the old. Tests load and correctness; avoid side effects.
Schema change in phases: add new, dual-write and backfill, switch reads, drop old in a later deploy. Keeps v1 and v2 both working.
Canary the build, flag the feature, expand/contract the schema, and always know how to roll back before you start.
